title: Service Boundaries Design
description: Learn to design effective service boundaries using business capabilities and bounded contexts.

data.text: Poor service boundaries are the leading cause of microservices failure. If boundaries are wrong, you end up with a distributed monolith—multiple services that are tightly coupled and must be changed together. Amazon, Google, and Uber all emphasize the importance of well-defined boundaries.

data.title: Steps to Design Boundaries
items: Identify business capabilities: What does the business do? (e.g., order management, inventory, billing)
Map domain concepts: Use Domain-Driven Design to find bounded contexts
Define data ownership: Each service should own its data exclusively
Evaluate coupling: Minimize synchronous calls between services
Consider team ownership: Align services with team structures

data.title: Warning Signs
items: You constantly need to change two services together
Services share the same database tables
One service depends on the internal data model of another
Deploying one service requires coordinating with another team
Service teams are fighting over ownership of the same domain concepts

data.title: The Distributed Monolith
data.text: A distributed monolith happens when services are so tightly coupled that they must be deployed and changed together. This is worse than a real monolith because you have the overhead of distributed systems without the autonomy benefits.

data.caption: Good vs bad service boundaries
data.definition:
graph LR
    subgraph Good[Good Boundaries]
        A[User Service] --> B[Own User DB]
        C[Order Service] --> D[Own Order DB]
        E[Payment Service] --> F[Own Payment DB]
        A -.->|Async Event| C
        C -.->|Async Event| E
    end
    subgraph Bad[Bad Boundaries]
        G[Service A] --> H[Shared DB]
        I[Service B] --> H
        G -->|Sync Call| I
        I -->|Sync Call| G
    end

data.title: Example: E-commerce Domain Boundaries
data.content: In an e-commerce system, good boundaries align with business capabilities. The User service manages profiles and authentication, the Order service handles order lifecycle, and the Payment service processes transactions. Each owns its own data.
data.code:
# Good service boundaries example
# UserService: manages user profiles, authentication, preferences
#   - Owns: users table, authentication tokens
#   - Exposes: GET /users, POST /users, POST /auth/login

# OrderService: manages order lifecycle
#   - Owns: orders, order_items tables
#   - Listens to: UserCreated event
#   - Exposes: GET /orders, POST /orders

# PaymentService: processes payments
#   - Owns: payments, invoices tables
#   - Listens to: OrderCreated event
#   - Exposes: POST /payments, GET /payments/{id}

items.question: What size should a service be?
items.answer: A service should be small enough to be owned by one team and large enough to deliver meaningful business value. If two people can fully understand it in a week, it is probably well-sized.

items.question: Can I change boundaries later?
items.answer: Yes, but it is expensive. Merging services is easier than splitting them, so err on the side of smaller services initially.

items.question: Should every team own one service?
items.answer: Ideally yes, but early on one team may own multiple services. The goal is to reduce cross-team coordination, not enforce a strict one-to-one mapping.

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: Service boundaries should align with business capabilities
Each service should own its data exclusively
Watch for signs of distributed monoliths
Use Domain-Driven Design to identify bounded contexts
data.takeaway: Good boundaries are the foundation of maintainable microservices; bad boundaries create distributed monoliths.
